Decided to try more aggressive prefix caching and adjust batch size for tail latency. Action items assigned for cost model update and a 24h throughput benchmark.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-10 09:30am PT | Duration 46m | Recorded | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Hannah (Redwood SE), Priya (Meridian ML), Liam (Infra), Sofia (CTO), Ethan (Product)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do a quick econ retrospective on the pilot so far, and then tune batching/caching. i'll kick off with the numbers we promised last week.
[00:18] Priya: great, thanks. quick note, we're on a weird network window this morning, so if audio cuts we'll rejoin.
[00:30] Daniel: no worries. i'll share screen after maya's overview - got the live dashboard and the token/sec per dollar calc.
[00:42] Maya: ok so headline, with the baseline config (r-infer-prod-v1, fp16, default batch 8) you folks are seeing roughly 12,400 tokens/sec per dollar at median load, but that hides the tail - p95 token issuance drops when we hit concurrent sessions. caching raised effective throughput by about 22% for the top-100 prompts.
[01:10] Priya: can you repeat the 22%? i thought our estimate was 15% last sync.
[01:15] Maya: yeah so last week we only counted static prompt caching. Daniel's new KV prefix caching count includes the subtle prefix hits so it bumped to 22% — there was some mislabeling in the dashboard previously.
[01:30] Daniel: we had a parsing issue where 'customer_profile:' prefix was split into two tokens intermittently, so some hits were undercounted — fixed that today.
[01:42] Liam: that split token problem rings a bell — we saw some odd cache miss spikes around 3am in the logs. that correlated with a deploy on your side?
[01:50] Hannah: there was a small rollout but it shouldn't affect cache keys. i think the split was from the tokenizer mismatch with their prompt templating; the fix normalizes spaces.
[02:05] Sofia: high level question — with the caching improvements, are we safe to move to the smaller model variant for cost savings? we care about >=98% parity on the eval.
[02:15] Daniel: we ran the smaller variant (r-infer-slim) across the eval set — delta is about 0.9% absolute on our NLU metric, but at high concurrency the smaller variant holds latency better; its quantization path seems more efficient.
[02:30] Priya: 0.9% might be acceptable, depends on which intents degrade. i'll take that to the product folks.
[02:36] Ethan: yeah we have a subset of intents that are basically revenue-critical, we'd need precision there.
[02:42] Maya: totally. back to econ — tokens/sec per dollar is one axis, tokens/sec per GPU-hour another. for the 24h run we recommended, we estimate a 28-35% cost saving if prefix caching hits stay at ~20% and we increase batch size to 12 during steady-state.
[03:05] Liam: increasing batch to 12 — what's the p99 impact? our SLA is p99 < 350ms.
[03:12] Daniel: good callout. with batch 12 we see p50 excellent, p99 shifts from ~310ms to ~390ms in peak tail on the hosted infra. but with KV cache applied aggressively the p99 reduces back to ~330ms in our simulations. so caching + slightly larger batches is the combo. there is a tradeoff for cold starts though.
[03:38] Priya: cold start being when? new user sessions?
[03:41] Daniel: yes, first requests that can't reuse past KV state. that path has higher latency; we can mitigate with small warm-up requests or a short-lived prefix cache.
[03:52] Sofia: is there any risk we'll see more errors if we push more batching? we can't accept higher generation truncations.
[03:58] Hannah: functionally no, batching just aggregates requests on the GPU; truncations would only surface if you push token limits or the model variant has different context handling. we've been conservative on max tokens per req.
[04:10] Maya: ok, quick demo — daniel, if you can show the dashboard slice for the last 48 hours?
[04:15] Daniel: sure. sharing. you can see here the cost-per-token curve by hour, and the cache hit histogram. note the big dip on Tuesday 02:00 when a template change invalidated a lot of entries.
[04:28] Priya: yes that was our template deploy where we accidentally included a trailing space, whoops.
[04:33] Maya: happens. good news is the cache warmed back within 45 minutes, which kept cumulative cost in check.
[04:40] Ethan: curious about how you're calculating 'effective tokens saved' — is that based purely on KV hits or do you factor in response length changes?
[04:48] Daniel: we use KV hits * avg response tokens saved, plus a small correction factor for truncated generations. it's an empirical model derived from the sample logs. i've attached the calculation in the sheet.
[05:00] Maya: the sheet link is in chat: https://redwood.ai/pilot-costs/meridian-weekly (note: not a real link in transcript).
[05:08] Priya: got it. thanks.
[05:12] Liam: quick infra question — if we go Private (VPC), what's the expected delta on tokens/sec/$ given our VM profile?
[05:20] Daniel: two components: networking overhead (small) and ability to pick instance types. on-prem or private can reduce cross-tenant scheduling overhead and give us more consistent p99s — that typically improves tokens/sec/$ by 5-12% depending on instance choice. but there's an ops cost tradeoff.
[05:38] Sofia: sounds reasonable. we need to get security docs too — SOC2, encrypt at rest, KMS — can you resend the compliance pack?
[05:46] Maya: yes sending post-call. action: i'll share the redwood compliance brief + SOC2 report link.
[05:52] Daniel: also note our audit logs include per-token tracing hooks (obfuscated text) if you need for debugging — low overhead.
[06:00] Priya: back to batching tradeoffs — can we do adaptive batching where we increase batch size when queue depth exceeds threshold?
[06:08] Daniel: absolutely — Redwood runtime supports adaptive batching policies today. you can set a latency SLO and it will dynamically adjust batch size within configured min/max. it's how we keep p99 stable while optimizing throughput.
[06:20] Liam: any precedent customers using adaptive batching in prod?
[06:23] Daniel: yes, a few fintech customers and one marketplace reduced token costs by ~18% with minimal p99 impact. we anonymized the case study in the docs.
[06:33] Priya: good. can we see the sample adaptive policy you'd recommend?
[06:36] Daniel: i'll add a recommended policy snippet to the shared sheet — e.g., min_batch 4, max_batch 14, latency_target 300ms, warmup_threshold 8 requests.
[06:46] Ethan: warmup threshold meaning?
[06:48] Daniel: if queue depth reaches 8, start scaling batch toward max. keeps tail low during spikes.
[06:55] Sofia: fine. another practical ask — how to monitor cost drift? we want alerts when tokens/$ falls below target.
[07:01] Maya: our console supports route-level cost alerts; we can set a rolling 6-hour tokens-per-dollar metric and trigger when delta > 10%. i'll put a recommended alert in the sheet.
[07:12] Priya: perfect.
[07:15] Maya: quick pause — any blockers from your side to run the 24h throughput with the new batch 12 + aggressive prefix caching?
[07:24] Priya: no blockers technically. scheduling-wise we'll run it Wednesday night to avoid daytime traffic.
[07:29] Liam: we'll need a little heads up so we can watch network egress and ensure NAT concurrent limits won't throttle.
[07:36] Maya: we'll give 48h heads up. action captured.
[07:40] Hannah: one more micro-optimization we recommend: token-aware prompt normalization to reduce tokenization variance across templates — that alone moved cache hit-rate up ~4% in our tests.
[07:52] Priya: can you give a concrete example?
[07:54] Hannah: strip trailing whitespace, normalize date formats, and replace long enumerations with placeholders pre-tokenized. we'll put examples in the sheet.
[08:05] Ethan: about cost math, the model variant switch to slim — what is the expected net unit change if we combine slim + caching + batch 12?
[08:12] Daniel: ballpark: slim alone gives ~18% cost reduction, caching ~22% observed (so combined naive would be ~34% but there is overlap). our model predicts net ~28-33% depending on hit-rate.
[08:27] Priya: okay that range helps. we'll need conservative planning numbers for the execs.
[08:31] Sofia: yes please include best/worst case in the sheet.
[08:35] Maya: will do.
[08:37] Priya: any concerns about quality regressions we should watch?
[08:40] Daniel: track top-5 revenue intents, run the eval daily against a rolling sample, and set a regression alert if any metric drops >0.5% absolute.
[08:51] Maya: adding: we also recommend a gradual canary rollout of the slim model at 10/30/60% traffic with automatic fallback to baseline if quality alerts fire.
[09:00] Liam: that helps with risk.
[09:03] Priya: ok, on the compliance docs — can you embed the network topology guidance for VPC peering? we had questions about CIDR conflicts.
[09:11] Daniel: yes, i'll include a short checklist and sample Terraform snippet for peering.
[09:17] Maya: let's summarize next steps — we'll list them in chat and in the sheet.
[09:22] Maya: recap: 1) Redwood sends updated cost model + batch/caching settings + compliance pack (maya). 2) Redwood shares KV cache histograms and policy snippet (daniel). 3) Meridian runs 24h throughput with batch 12 + aggressive prefix caching and shares logs (priya/liam). 4) Schedule private deployment checklist review (liam + maya).
[09:40] Priya: sounds good. question — would you recommend we switch to slim immediately in the pilot or wait for the 24h run?
[09:46] Daniel: wait for the run and do a canary. immediate switch is higher risk.
[09:50] Sofia: agree. canary then decide.
[09:52] Maya: ok thanks everyone — i'll drop the sheet and compliance links, and we'll reconvene after the 24h run.
[09:58] Priya: thanks, bye.
[10:00] Meeting end.

Notes: Transcript contains some ASR artifacts (tokenizer spelled as 'tokenizer' sometimes 'tokenizerer', occasional speaker mislabeling). Shared artifacts: meridian-weekly spreadsheet (cost model), cache-histograms.csv, redwood-compliance-pack.pdf.
